mappings.note: An imagined letter describing daily life in Gupta Pataliputra - social and cultural history of a period. No LO in this frame covers everyday life, so the goal is the honest fit.
Chandragupta II as Vikramaditya - a dynastic recall. Not LO-124, because the title is asked as a name rather than analysed as a claim to authority.
Tests the claim that peace enabled Gupta literature, science and art. A judgement about the conditions of a cultural flowering, so the goal rather than an administrative measure.
A role play of a Gupta court with king, minister and scholars. The scene is cultural rather than a study of administration, so CG-SST2 rather than LO-124.
Matches Kanchipuram, Ujjayini, Udayagiri, Ajanta and Pataliputra to what each is known for. Historical geography across art, learning and politics, so the goal.
Who the Pallavas were and where they ruled. Dynastic and regional recall; no governance is examined.
A field visit to a museum or heritage site, reporting on artefacts and significance. Working from material remains is the goal's 'types of sources' clause.
The Gupta age as India's 'classical age'. A period characterisation under the goal.
The Iron Pillar's rust resistance as evidence of advanced metallurgy. Technological history; LO-126 covers the construction of temples, tombs and mosques, which a free-standing pillar is not.
'Maharajadhiraja' as great king of kings, asserting supremacy over subordinate rulers. Imperial authority, so LO-124 rather than a plain vocabulary recall.
The Lichchhavi marriage as the alliance that consolidated early Gupta power - a strategy of statecraft. Not CG-SST2, because the marriage is analysed for what it did politically.

Samudragupta annexing in the north but reinstating southern kings as tributaries is a deliberate difference in method of control. Not LO-125, because it is one ruler's two strategies rather than two rulers compared.
Harisena as the author of the Prayaga Prashasti - identifying who produced a key source. The goal's sources clause.
'Dharani-bandha' as the ambition to unify the earth under one rule - an imperial aim recorded in a prashasti. Not CG-SST2, because the term is read as a claim to universal dominion.

Faxian's report of Vaishya charitable houses read as evidence of community philanthropy - social history from a traveller's account. Not LO-124, because the answer explicitly contrasts community effort with state provision.
Defines 'prashasti' as a eulogistic inscription. A statement about a class of source, so the goal rather than LO-124.
Grand titles like chakravartin used to project supreme power over other rulers. Imperial self-presentation, the same lane as the maharajadhiraja item.
Prabhavati Gupta's marriage into the Vakatakas as a strategically important alliance. Statecraft, so LO-124.
Matches Gupta-era figures to their fields, keyed on Varahamihira. Intellectual history under the goal.
Accepts the classical-age label but rejects invasions as its cause, restoring peace and stability. A judgement about why a cultural flowering happened.
Matches Gupta achievements to their fields and rejects the Aryabhatiya as a work on drama. Intellectual and technological history.

Statements on the Gupta capital, their trade and the false claim of exclusive Vaishnavism. Mixed period recall, so the goal rather than the religious-policy reading given to the assertion-reason item on tolerance.
Aryabhata's claim that the Earth spins on its axis. Scientific history under the goal.
Places Kamarupa in the Brahmaputra valley. Historical geography of a contemporary kingdom.
Defines a regent as one who governs in a monarch's place, with Prabhavati Gupta as the example. An office of governance, so LO-124.
The Brihat Samhita's coverage extending to weather forecasting. Scientific and textual history.
Copper-plate land grants read as a practice of permanent official record-keeping. Administrative method, which LO-124 names.
'Ghatikas' as Pallava centres of higher learning. Educational and cultural history; not an administrative institution of the state.
Governing provinces by granting land and authority to local chiefs in return for loyalty and revenue is the Gupta method of control. Squarely LO-124.
Matches scholars to their works, keyed on Charaka. A sources-and-authors item under the goal.

Gupta rulers being personally Vaishnava yet patronising Buddhism and Jainism is a deliberate policy, and the reason ties it to the period's vibrancy. Read as a measure of rule, as with the patronage items in the neighbouring chapters; LO-127 would need a new movement to be emerging.
Links Gupta achievements to their fields and rejects the Iron Pillar as chiefly architectural, since its fame is metallurgical. Technological history, not LO-126.
Ayurveda as the traditional medical system codified in this era. Intellectual and textual history under the goal.
Names the Vakatakas as co-patrons of Ajanta. A patronage-and-dynasty recall; the item never asks about the caves' style or technique, which would make it LO-126.
The veena coin read as evidence of Samudragupta's cultural patronage - inference from a numismatic source. Not LO-124, because no measure of rule is inferred.
Identifies Aryabhata from planetary formulas, the length of the year and eclipse explanations. Scientific history under the goal.
Weighs Huna invasions, breakaway regional rulers and succession conflict as causes of Gupta decline against a false one. Reasoning about the limits of imperial control, so LO-124.
Kanchipuram as the Pallava capital and centre of learning. Historical geography; the temples are mentioned but no architectural development is described.
A cluster of clues - temples, astronomy, Sanskrit poetry - has to be resolved to the Gupta period. Period identification under the goal.
Rejects Mohenjo-daro as a Gupta-era centre because it belongs to the Harappan age. Chronological placement across periods.
